title: Preamble: Four Color Theorem Status and Lean 4 Gap Analysis
content: The module docstring (lines 5-43) provides a comprehensive survey of the Four Color Theorem formalization landscape. The 4CT was first proved by Appel–Haken (1977) with massive computer assistance and formalized in Coq by Gonthier (2005) in ~60,000 lines. The Lean 4 status section identifies critical gaps: planar graph definitions are missing from Mathlib, and Euler's formula V-E+F=2 is not yet formalized. The file proves what is currently achievable: small cases (≤4 vertices) and basic coloring API. This serves as the starting point for any future full 4CT formalization in Lean 4.
mathContext: The Four Color Theorem: every planar graph $G$ satisfies $\chi(G) \leq 4$. The proof requires: (1) every minimal counterexample is an internally 6-connected triangulation; (2) all such triangulations contain one of 633 unavoidable configurations; (3) each is reducible. Steps (2)-(3) involve ~$10^9$ computer-checked cases. Mathlib's gap: no planar graph type, no Euler formula $V - E + F = 2$, no Birkhoff reducibility, no discharge method.

title: Colorability Basics: The Lean 4 API for Graph Coloring
content: Four theorems establish the foundation: `colorable_of_le` uses `Colorable.mono : G.Colorable n → n ≤ m → G.Colorable m` (monotonicity). `empty_colorable` uses `isEmptyElim` — for an empty type V, any function from V is vacuously defined. `edgeless_one_colorable` constructs the coloring explicitly: `fun _ => ⟨0, by omega⟩` sends every vertex to color 0 (the only fin 1 element), and the adjacency condition is vacuously true since the graph has no edges (SimpleGraph.Bot.not_adj). `colorable_of_fintype` is a one-line delegation to Mathlib's `G.colorable_of_fintype`, which constructs a coloring by assigning distinct colors to each vertex (index by Fintype).

title: Small Cases: The Easy 4CT is Trivial by Monotonicity
content: `four_colorable_small` (card V ≤ 4 → 4-colorable) is a one-liner: `G.colorable_of_fintype.mono hV`. Since V has ≤4 vertices, G is Fintype.card V ≤ 4 colorable, and monotonicity gives 4-colorable. `four_colorable_of_bipartite` (2-colorable → 4-colorable) is also one line: `h.mono (by omega)`. The mathematical content of the genuine 4CT is that PLANAR graphs are 4-colorable — these trivial cases avoid planarity entirely and do not represent genuine progress toward the 4CT. They are best understood as sanity checks that the coloring API works correctly.
mathContext: For graphs with $\le 4$ vertices: any $n$-vertex graph is $n$-colorable (just assign distinct colors). For bipartite graphs: 2-colorability is equivalent to having no odd cycles (König's theorem), giving 2-colorability directly. Both are special cases of 4-colorability by monotonicity. The genuine 4CT claim is about PLANAR graphs with arbitrarily many vertices — a fundamentally different statement requiring planarity theory.

title: PlanarHasLowDegreeVertex: The Key Ingredient for Five Color
content: `PlanarHasLowDegreeVertex` is defined as `def ... : Prop := True` — a placeholder requiring planar graph infrastructure. The mathematical content: every simple planar graph has a vertex of degree ≤ 5. Proof sketch from Euler's formula: for a connected planar graph, V - E + F = 2. Each face has ≥ 3 edges and each edge borders ≤ 2 faces, so 3F ≤ 2E, giving F ≤ 2E/3. Substituting: V - E + 2E/3 ≥ 2, so E ≤ 3V - 6. Thus average degree = 2E/V < 6, giving a vertex of degree ≤ 5. This is the induction hypothesis for the Five Color Theorem proof.
mathContext: Euler's formula: $V - E + F = 2$ for connected planar graphs. Handshaking for faces: $\sum_f \deg(f) = 2E$ with $\deg(f) \ge 3$ for all faces, giving $3F \le 2E$. Combined: $V - E + \frac{2E}{3} \ge 2$, so $E \le 3V - 6$. Average vertex degree $= 2E/V \le (6V-12)/V < 6$, so $\min \deg \le 5$. For the Five Color Theorem: by induction, remove a minimum-degree vertex $v$ (degree $\le 5$), 5-color the rest, then reinsert $v$ — if its neighbors use $\le 4$ colors, color $v$ with the 5th.

title: Feasibility Assessment: ~43K Lines Across 5 Components
content: The tabulated estimate breaks the 4CT into 5 components: (1) graph theory basics (~2K lines, partially in Mathlib); (2) planar embeddings (~6K lines, not in Mathlib); (3) reducibility framework (~12K lines); (4) unavoidable configurations — 633 in RSST 1997 — (~15K lines); (5) computational kernel (~8K lines, candidate for native_decide). The three approaches differ mainly in how they handle the computational kernel: Coq port (~43K total), native_decide-based (~potentially shorter), RSST route (favored by Gonthier for its 633 vs 1936 configurations). The < 5% current status reflects only the basic coloring theorems being in Mathlib.
mathContext: The Robertson-Sanders-Seymour-Thomas (1997) proof: (1) every minimal 4CT counterexample is an internally 6-connected triangulation; (2) such triangulations contain one of 633 'unavoidable' configurations; (3) each configuration is 'reducible' (Birkhoff 1913 notion: replacing the configuration with a smaller graph preserves the property that the graph is a minimal counterexample — contradiction). Steps (2) and (3) are verified computationally. `native_decide` in Lean 4 compiles the decision procedure to native code, checking in seconds what takes hours symbolically.
